In addition to these demands which can be met with relatively little difficulty, there will be large increases in housing demand. Table 29 to 32 in Appendix I, show the number of new households each year in each of the communities for the converging Labor Force Participation Rate, both low and moderate Alternative Futures, and Baseline and Scenario 1 conditions. These indicate that for moderate development of regional coal (Alternative Future-2) and a low level of development by Westmoreland Resources (Scenario 1) total housing increases of 672, 610 337, and 30 units will be required in Hardin, Crow Agency, Lodge Grass, and Wyola, respectively over the 25 year period. These changes amount to 11-40 new houses per year in Crow Agency, 7-17 in Lodge Grass, and 1-2 in Wyola. The demand will grow steadily (Figure III-6) each year until the higher annual figure is reached by the end of the 25 year period. In the three communities other than Hardin, these changes are almost entirely as a result of natural population increase.
Figure III-8 shows that the effect of Westmoreland mining activity on housing demand in Hardin is contingent upon the baseline situation at the time of this activity. If Westmoreland is the only mine operating (AF-1), the necessary labor force can be supplied almost entirely from local residents. Thus, limited in-migration would raise the housing demand only slightly. If, on the other hand, there are one or two mines operating concurrently with Westmoreland's activity (AF-2), the impact will be much greater. In this event, the local labor supply will have been utilized and substantial in-migration will occur, especially in the late 1970's and early 1980's.
